title: Ardhanarishvara: the lord who is half woman
hookLine: the creator's world won't grow until Shiva appears as half himself, half the goddess: God and God's power in one body
carry: shiva and shakti are never two
tomorrow: why is the dancer's face so calm?

lines: RIGHT SIDE: MATTED HAIR, A SNAKE.
ONE FIGURE, SPLIT DOWN THE MIDDLE.
cards: A bronze figure stands with a slight sway at the hip. On its right side: a man's flat chest, matted hair piled high, a snake for an earring.
On the left: a woman's breast, smooth braided hair, a round earring, an anklet on the foot, the hip curving out. Not two figures standing close. One figure, split down the middle.
This is Ardhanarishvara, and the Shiva Purana tells a story about why the creator needed to see it.

teach.b: Brahma, the creator, has a problem. He makes beings from his own mind, and they don't multiply. The world stays small.
So he does tapas, and Shiva appears to him in this form, half himself and half the goddess. Brahma bows and asks the goddess side for help.

She gives a power of her own so that creation can go on, and in the story the world begins to grow through women and men together. So the picture isn't a riddle. It's an answer: creation doesn't go forward on one half.
The name says it plainly: ardha, half, nari, woman, ishvara, lord. The lord who is half woman. Some Shaiva teachers put it this way: Shiva and Shakti, the god and his power, are never really two.

One poet found an image for it. At the opening of his long poem the Raghuvamsha, Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined, he says, like a word and its meaning. Try separating those.

teach.h: LIKE A WORD AND ITS MEANING.
teach.b: A word with no meaning is noise; a meaning with no word can't be said.
So the teaching is plain: in Shaiva and Shakta thought, God isn't only male, and Shakti, the power that makes and moves the world, isn't a lesser half. It's God's own power.
It's why, in Hindi, a wife can be called ardhangini, the half of the body, and why many rites are done by husband and wife together.

teach.h: SHIVA AND SHAKTI ARE NEVER TWO.
teach.b: That's the last selection from the Shiva Purana: Sati and Parvati, who circled Shiva through all those stories, now standing in one body with him.

how: Ardhanarishvara, Shiva as half man and half woman, appears in temple sculpture and bronzes and is worshiped as a picture of Shiva and Shakti inseparable; Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha opens by bowing to Parvati and Shiva joined like a word and its meaning.

o: a book of Shiva's stories, closing on the lord who is half woman
a manual telling temple sculptors how to cast bronze gods
a temple song sung when a bride and groom first meet

games.q: the half-woman lord — tap the pairs.

s: Ardhanarishvara is two figures standing side by side
it's one figure, split down the middle: half Shiva, half the goddess.
in the story, Brahma's creation wasn't growing
he did tapas, and Shiva appeared to him as half woman.
Kalidasa compared Shiva and Parvati to a word and its meaning
at the opening of the Raghuvamsha.

games.q: you're Brahma. the beings you make don't multiply, and Shiva has appeared to you as half man, half woman. whom do you ask for help?
o: no one; you try again alone.
games.why: Brahma asks the goddess side, and she gives a power of her own so that creation goes on. one half alone couldn't do it.

practice: Bring your attention to the right side of the body, the hand, the shoulder, the foot, and breathe there a few breaths; then move to the left side and breathe there.
Then let the line down the middle go soft, and feel the whole body breathing as one thing. If you pray, you can say the names Shiva and Shakti, or the name of God you use, and let them rest together.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Purana. Today's selection, and the last: Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman, the answer when Brahma's world wouldn't grow.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Ardhanarishvara, from ardha (half), nari (woman) and ishvara (lord): the lord who is half woman.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva and Shakti are never two. Tomorrow, Shiva dances. That's the Shiva Purana, gathered up.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Shatarudra Samhita (the Ardhanarishvara form appearing to Brahma)
